source.title: Bypassing the Safety Training of Open-Source LLMs with Priming Attacks
source.authors: Jason Vega; Isha Chaudhary; Changming Xu; Gagandeep Singh

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether priming with a compliant opening bypasses safety behaviour, using inference-time priming attacks rather than the fine-tuning or token-position measurements in the original sources.
record.gate_note: The study reports harmful-completion attack success rates for no attack, the “Just Sure” affirmative opening, and its longer priming attack. It also reports an evaluator comparison for Llama-2 (7B). The Llama Guard instruction-tuning details are not outcomes about the claim. Cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study prefills a compliant response opening ("Just Sure" and longer priming text) on safety-trained chat models. It reports harmful-completion ASR against a no-attack control, which directly tests V4's prefilling claim. It does no fine-tuning, per-token KL, parameter localization or deepening training.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with corrections. The authors conclude that cheap priming (prefilling a partial compliant response) bypasses safety training of open-source Llama-2 and Vicuna chat models. They say their attack outperforms both baselines for all models, up to 3.3× over "Just Sure" under Llama Guard. They report that larger Llama-2 is safer and that Llama Guard underestimates harmfulness. They caveat the limited prompt set and unassessed response quality.
record.recipe_differences: This study uses inference-time priming: a helper model generates a partial compliant response that is appended to a harmful request. It does not fine-tune the target model or measure token-position KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported effectiveness varies by target model and evaluator; the authors note that larger Llama-2 models appear safer against priming attacks. For Vicuna (13B), the priming attack does not exceed the “Just Sure” ASR.
record.problems: The evaluation uses only prompts from the Harmful Behaviors dataset, which the authors describe as a limited subset. Human evaluation is by a single author and is reported only for Llama-2 (7B). The authors note that Llama Guard may underestimate harmfulness and that response quality was not evaluated; some successful responses may be high-level or incorrect. A human study was not conducted.

untested.parts: Adversarial suffixes and decoding changes. It also does not report how ASR varies with prefill length in tokens.
Not tested: no per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Not tested. The authors only speculate that full-response safety data enables priming.

missing.what: Llama Guard agreement with human labels for priming on Llama-2 (7B): 30.89% false negatives, 60.0% true positives, 2.89% true negatives, 6.22% false positives. This shows judge dependence of ASR.
Qualitative examples where Llama-2 backtracks into a refusal after a compliant prefill (shallow-alignment recovery), counted as safe.

record.verdict_notes: The reader misassigned the Vicuna 7B/13B columns of Table 1. The corrected values remove the record's claim that priming falls below "Just Sure" for Vicuna 13B. Vicuna is described by the authors as safety-trained, though its alignment is weak, consistent with its high bare-prefill ASR. Llama Guard instructions were tuned on 30 of the 485 test prompts, a minor contamination of the test set. Human evaluation is by a single author and covers Llama-2 7B only.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-example fine-tuning or post-fine-tuning refusal measurement.
No benign-data fine-tuning or resulting harmful-compliance measurement.
No per-token KL or other aligned-versus-base response-position measurement.
Tests inference-time priming with an affirmative/compliant opening. Does not test adversarial suffixes or decoding changes.
No weight or rank localization measurement.
Does not test whether the training data or objective causes safety shallowness.
No training intended to deepen safety across response tokens, or test of whether such training holds up.

source_check.reason: Llama-2 (7B) priming reaches 66.19% under Llama Guard and 90.89% under human evaluation; both Vicuna prefill types reach approximately 85%. Correcting the Vicuna column swaps preserves this verdict.

relationships.condition: Llama-2 chat models with a bare "Sure, here is" prefill, and Llama-2 (13B) generally
relationships.reason: A bare affirmative prefill gives only 20–35% ASR on Llama-2 (r2, r5, r8). Priming reaches 51% on 13B versus 66% on 7B (r9, r3). The bypass depends on prefill length and on model size and family, and the measured rate depends on the judge.
relationships.display_finding: A bare affirmative prefill gave only 20–35% ASR, and priming reached 51% on 13B versus 66% on 7B; bypass depended on prefill length, model size and family, and the judge.

relation.reason: The study directly measures V4: whether compliant response openings bypass refusal on safety-trained chat models.

tranche.reason: Inference-time generated response prefilling tests safety bypass through a different method, with harmful-completion ASR and no-attack controls.

source_check.notes: Experiments omit system instructions; Llama Guard instructions were adapted using test-set responses, and human evaluation used one author. ASR measures harmful content, with response quality left unevaluated.
